blocks.prompt: The Iceberg That Hides Most of Itself
blocks.text: An iceberg looks like a small white hill on the sea. It is not small. Under the water there is much more ice. Nine parts out of ten are hiding down there. You only see one part. Icebergs are made of snow. Snow fell on a cold land long ago. More snow fell on top. It packed down hard and turned into ice. The ice slid slowly to the sea. Then a big piece broke off and floated away. That piece is an iceberg. It is not salty. It is made of fresh water, like rain.

blocks.prompt: Where an Iceberg Comes From
blocks.text: An iceberg does not start in the sea. It starts as snow, high on a cold mountain or on a wide sheet of ice like the one that covers Greenland. Snow falls and does not melt. More snow falls on top of it. Year after year, the weight presses the old snow down until it packs into solid ice. That ice becomes a glacier, and a glacier is a river that moves too slowly to watch. It creeps downhill toward the ocean. When the front of the glacier reaches the water, the sea lifts it and cracks it. Great slabs snap off with a boom and splash into the ocean. Scientists call that calving. The floating piece is an iceberg. Now the strangest part. Ice is a little lighter than sea water, but only a little. So an iceberg floats with about nine tenths of itself under the surface. The white hill you can see is the small part. The rest is a huge blue shape in the dark water below, wider than the top and much deeper than it looks.

blocks.prompt: The Tip of the Iceberg
blocks.text: You have probably heard someone say that a problem is only the tip of the iceberg. The phrase comes from real physics. Ice is slightly less dense than sea water. Glacier ice weighs about 917 kilograms per cubic meter, while cold sea water weighs about 1,025. Because the ice is lighter, it floats. Because the difference is small, it only just floats. Roughly one tenth of an iceberg rides above the surface. The other nine tenths hang below, out of sight. That hidden ice is old. The snow that made it may have fallen before the pyramids were built. As the snow was buried and squeezed, it trapped tiny bubbles of the air that was around at the time. When an iceberg melts, those bubbles pop free and fizz. Sailors call the sound bergy seltzer, and you can hear it across open water. Squeezing changes the color too. Ice packed hard enough loses most of its bubbles, and light travels deep inside it. The ice soaks up red light and lets blue escape, so old, dense ice glows a startling blue. Young, bubbly ice scatters every color at once and looks plain white. An iceberg is not a peaceful thing. It melts unevenly, mostly from underneath, where the water is warmer than the air. As it thins, its balance shifts, and without warning the whole mountain can roll over. A rolling iceberg throws waves big enough to swamp a boat, which is one more reason ships keep their distance.

blocks.prompt: Ninety Percent Below
blocks.text: On the night of April 14, 1912, a lookout on the Titanic saw a dark shape ahead and had less than a minute to react. What the ship struck was not rock. It was compressed snow. Every iceberg begins as snowfall on a glacier or an ice sheet, and the ice that opened the hull of the largest ship in the world had been sitting on Greenland for thousands of years before it slid into the sea. An iceberg floats because glacier ice is slightly less dense than sea water, but the margin is thin. About nine tenths of its mass stays submerged. That is the arithmetic behind the phrase the tip of the iceberg, and it is also why icebergs are so dangerous. The visible peak tells you almost nothing about the shape underneath, which can reach outward for hundreds of meters in a direction you cannot see. The two polar regions build different bergs. Greenland's glaciers squeeze through narrow fjords and shatter as they go, producing jagged, top heavy pinnacle bergs that drift south into the shipping lanes of the North Atlantic. Antarctica does something else. Its floating ice shelves crack along the front and release flat topped tabular icebergs the size of counties. Iceberg B-15 broke away from the Ross Ice Shelf in 2000 and measured about 11,000 square kilometers, close to the area of Jamaica. The Titanic disaster changed the ocean. Nations met, wrote the first international agreement on safety at sea, and in 1914 created the International Ice Patrol. The United States Coast Guard has flown it every season since, and the patrol reports that no ship following its published iceberg limits has ever struck one. Icebergs are not only hazards. As one drifts and melts, it releases the rock flour and iron dust its parent glacier scraped off the mountains. That dust feeds phytoplankton, and satellites have photographed green blooms trailing behind big bergs like wakes. The larger stones sink when the ice lets go of them. Geologists find these dropstones sitting in fine ocean mud thousands of kilometers from any coast, and use them to map where ice once traveled. An iceberg is a piece of a continent's memory, drifting away from the place that made it. It carries ancient air, ancient dust, and the record of a snowfall nobody witnessed. Most of that record is under the water, where nobody looks.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: 917 divided by 1,025 is about 0.895
Calving: the slab breaking off a glacier front
Trapped bubbles hold the air of ancient years
Bubble free ice absorbs red, so it looks blue
Dropstones mark where icebergs once melted
Greenland now sheds hundreds of billions of tons a year

blocks.prompt: The Tip of the Iceberg: What Floating Ice Is Evidence Of
blocks.text: Everyone knows the phrase. When someone says a problem is only the tip of the iceberg, they mean the visible part is the small part. The phrase has survived for a century because the physics behind it is exact, and the physics is worth knowing. Glacier ice has a density of roughly 917 kilograms per cubic meter. Cold sea water is denser, at about 1,025. Divide one by the other and you get 0.895. An iceberg therefore floats with about ninety percent of its mass below the surface and ten percent above, and no iceberg gets a vote in the matter. The ratio is not a rule of thumb. It is a consequence of what the two substances weigh. An iceberg is not frozen sea. It is compressed weather. Snow falls on Greenland or Antarctica and does not melt. More snow buries it. Under the growing weight the flakes lose their points, pack together, and after decades or centuries become solid ice. That ice flows. A glacier is a river that moves too slowly to watch, though the fastest ones travel tens of meters a day, and when its front reaches the ocean the water lifts and flexes it until slabs break away. The word for that is calving, and it is how a continent sheds its ice. What floats away is an archive. Sealed inside the ice are bubbles of the atmosphere from the year the snow fell, unchanged since. Scientists drill ice cores for exactly this reason: the bubbles are samples of old air, and there is no other way to get one. When an iceberg melts, those bubbles burst and hiss, a sound sailors named bergy seltzer. Ice that has had its bubbles squeezed out turns a startling blue, because dense ice absorbs red light and lets blue pass through. White ice is simply young ice, still full of air. Icebergs carry rock as well. A glacier grinds the mountains it crosses into flour and hauls the fragments downhill, and when the ice melts the stones fall to the seafloor. Geologists thousands of kilometers from any coast find dropstones sitting in fine ocean mud where no stone has any business being. The iron in that dust fertilizes the water, and satellites have photographed plankton blooms streaming behind drifting bergs. Now the part that makes people uneasy. It is tempting to watch an iceberg melt and picture the ocean rising as it goes. That is not how it works. A floating iceberg has already displaced its own weight in water, so its melting changes sea level almost not at all. The moment that mattered happened earlier, and quietly, when the ice left the land. Calving is the transfer. Everything after is drift. This is why glaciologists count icebergs instead of mourning them. The berg itself is a receipt. It records how much ice a glacier has handed to the ocean, and the rate of that handover is the number that governs coastlines. Greenland now loses hundreds of billions of tons of ice a year, and much of it departs as icebergs crowding down fjords on the west coast, including Ilulissat, whose glacier is the one most often named as the source of the berg the Titanic met. So the idiom is right, but not in the way people use it. The hidden nine tenths is not the frightening part. The frightening part is what the visible tenth is evidence of: a continent quietly emptying itself into the sea, one white mountain at a time.
